Read About Bogotá

A city built on gold, salt and a single afternoon of violence that rewrote a continent — 2,640 meters up, and still climbing.

A city that starts in the clouds

Bogotá sits at 2,640 meters above sea level, on a high plateau the Spanish called the Sabana de Bogotá, ringed by the eastern hills that end abruptly at Monserrate. Only La Paz and Quito sit higher among the world's capitals. The air here is noticeably thin — visitors feel it on the first flight of stairs, long before they feel it on the Monserrate cable car — and the light at this elevation has a clarity that lowland cities never quite manage. Afternoon storms roll off the hills most days, drench the city for twenty minutes, and clear. Locals call the resulting light "la luz de Bogotá," and it is the first thing many photographers notice.

The plateau was never empty. Long before Europeans arrived, it was the heartland of the Muisca Confederation, a loose federation of chiefdoms that farmed the fertile savanna and mined salt from the hills — the same salt that, centuries later, would be hollowed into the underground cathedral at Zipaquirá.

The gold that became a legend

The Muisca were expert goldsmiths, and their most important ritual is the reason half of Spanish South America was mapped by treasure hunters who never found what they were looking for. When a new zipa — a Muisca ruler — was installed, he was covered in gold dust and ferried out onto Lake Guatavita, north of the city, on a ceremonial raft. Attendants threw gold ornaments and emeralds into the water as offerings while the gilded ruler washed the dust from his skin. Spanish colonists who heard secondhand, badly translated accounts of "the gilded one" turned a coronation ceremony into a rumor of a lost city of gold, and spent the better part of two centuries searching the continent for El Dorado.

The gold raft in Museo del Oro's vault is the closest thing that exists to physical proof the legend was real — it just wasn't a city.

The most complete surviving depiction of that ceremony — a small gold raft carrying the zipa and his attendants, cast by Muisca goldsmiths sometime before the conquest — sits today in the vault of the Museo del Oro, a short walk from Plaza de Bolívar. It is one of roughly 34,000 gold pieces in the museum's collection, the largest assembly of pre-Hispanic goldwork anywhere in the world, and it is the nearest thing to physical proof that the El Dorado legend began as something real: not a city, but a ceremony, misheard and magnified by men who wanted very badly to believe in gold cities.

Founded on a Thursday, in a churchyard

The Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada founded Santa Fe de Bogotá on August 6, 1538, on a stretch of high ground the Muisca had called Bacatá. Local tradition holds that the first Mass was said at the small plaza now known as Chorro de Quevedo, in what is today La Candelaria — the colonial core that still anchors the city center. The streets Quesada laid out there, narrow and steep and lined with red-tiled colonial houses, are largely the same streets visitors walk today between Plaza de Bolívar and the base of Monserrate.

Bogotá spent the following two and a half centuries as a Spanish colonial capital, then became the seat of Gran Colombia's independence movement in the early 1800s. Simón Bolívar lived at the Quinta de Bolívar, on the eastern edge of the old city, in the intervals between military campaigns; the house was a gift from a grateful republic, and it still holds his personal effects. The presidential palace, Casa de Nariño, stands a few blocks from where the republic's first congress convened, and Colombia's president still works there today.

The afternoon that changed the country

On April 9, 1948, a Liberal Party leader and leading presidential candidate named Jorge Eliécer Gaitán was shot dead on a downtown street, a few blocks from where he had just left his law office. Within hours, the killing had ignited a ten-hour riot that gutted much of downtown Bogotá — streetcars burned, colonial buildings that had stood for three centuries were destroyed, and by the time the fires went out, more than two thousand people were dead. Bogotanos still call it El Bogotazo.

The riot's aftershocks spread into the countryside and hardened into a period Colombians call La Violencia — a low-grade civil war between Liberals and Conservatives that ran for roughly a decade and left hundreds of thousands dead. Historians trace the roots of Colombia's much longer, later conflict — the one that produced FARC and decades of guerrilla war — back to that single April afternoon. Much of what downtown Bogotá looks like today, including stretches of the modern Carrera Séptima, was rebuilt in its wake.

Walls that talk back

Bogotá's other defining visual language arrived far more recently, and on nobody's official orders. Through the 2000s, the city had some of the harshest anti-graffiti enforcement in South America — until the 2011 police killing of a teenage graffiti artist named Diego Felipe Becerra, misreported at first as a gang shooting, set off public outrage that forced the city to decriminalize street art almost overnight. What followed was one of the more remarkable urban transformations in the region: entire blocks of La Candelaria and Chapinero became open-air galleries, and Bogotá is now considered one of the street-art capitals of the world, drawing muralists from across the Americas to paint walls the police once scrubbed clean by morning.

A single killing in 2011 turned Bogotá's hardest anti-graffiti laws into some of the most permissive in South America.

The murals are not incidental decoration. Many address the same history the rest of the city tries to move past quietly — La Violencia, the drug era, the disappeared — in a medium the government can no longer easily erase. Walking the guide's own route through La Candelaria means walking through a rolling, unofficial memorial that repaints itself every few months.

Salt, before gold

An hour north of the city, the Muisca were mining rock salt at Zipaquirá for at least a thousand years before Quesada arrived — salt was currency on the savanna long before the Spanish brought gold fever with them. The mine is still active. Deep inside it, miners carved a Catholic chapel out of the salt rock in the 1930s so workers could pray without climbing back to the surface; when that structure became unsafe, the current Salt Cathedral was carved further down and consecrated in 1995, a full basilica hollowed entirely out of halite two hundred meters underground. It remains one of the most-visited sites in Colombia outside the capital, and the guide's own Train Day ends there, on the same heritage line Bogotanos have been riding out to Zipaquirá since the railway's steam era.

The city today

Bogotá's reputation abroad still lags a couple of decades behind its reality. The worst years of the drug era emptied the streets of Zona Rosa and Chapinero after dark; today those same streets hold some of the most ambitious restaurant openings in South America, and Bogotá chefs are increasingly cited alongside Lima and Mexico City as the region's most interesting kitchens. The TransMilenio bus rapid transit system, one of the largest of its kind in the world, moves more than two million riders a day through a city that had almost no mass transit thirty years ago. A long-delayed metro line is finally under construction.

What hasn't changed is the altitude, the afternoon rain, and the particular quality of light that made Muisca priests build ceremonies around gold and water in the first place. Give the first day here more time than the itinerary suggests — the thin air asks for it — and the rest of the trip tends to fall into place on its own.
